title: SvelteKit Shallow Routing: pushState & Modal State Sync

progressiveExplaining.eli5: A hotel uses a guest registry (the URL) to record which room a visitor is in. Normally, changing the registry entry means actually moving the guest to a different room (loading new page data). Shallow routing is writing a note in the registry WITHOUT moving anyone: the entry says 'visitor is viewing the photo', but no new room was prepared — the same page just records the state. When the visitor closes the photo, the note is erased and the registry goes back to the original entry, without anyone being relocated.
progressiveExplaining.junior: Shallow routing updates the URL without running load functions or triggering a navigation. In SvelteKit: import { pushState } from '$app/navigation'; pushState(url, state);. This changes the address bar and adds a history entry, but does NOT call load, so no data is re-fetched and no component re-renders from the router. Use it for modal/drawer state that you want reflected in the URL (shareable, back-button-closable) without a real page change. To close: pushState back to the original URL, or use the browser's back button (the history entry exists). Read the state via $page.url or $page.state.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, shallow routing separates URL state from data loading: pushState writes a new entry into the history stack and updates $page (url and state) without invoking the navigation pipeline (no load, no component re-creation). This is ideal for ephemeral UI state that must be URL-representable — modals, filters, selected tabs — where a full navigation would be wasteful and disruptive. The state argument (pushState(url, { modal: 'photo' })) stores arbitrary serializable data in the history entry, retrievable from $page.state. Combining shallow routes with modals gives back-button-close behavior: the previous history entry is the closed state.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: pushState in SvelteKit wraps the browser's history.pushState: it constructs the new URL, calls history.pushState(state, '', url), and notifies the router to update the reactive $page store (url, params, state) WITHOUT running the load pipeline or reconciling the component tree. The router distinguishes this from a normal navigation by the absence of a load trigger. The History API itself stores the state object on the entry; SvelteKit reads it back into $page.state on popstate/back navigation. Because no load runs, the page's data stays intact — only the URL and state change. This makes the URL a first-class container for ephemeral UI state with zero data-fetching cost.

rosettaStone.react: React Router's history.pushState and URL-search-param state patterns mirror shallow routing.
rosettaStone.angular: Angular's Location.go / Router without navigation events approximates it.
rosettaStone.vue: Vue Router's router.replace with same-route params is the analogue.

codeComparison.title: Full navigation for a modal vs shallow routing
codeComparison.summary: Navigating to a modal URL re-runs load and recreates the page; shallow routing updates only the URL/state, keeping the page and data intact.

legacyOrBad.label: Navigate to a real route for the modal
legacyOrBad.snippet: await goto('/photos/1'); // ❌ OLD: full navigation — load runs, page re-renders

fullFile.code:
<script>
  import { goto } from '$app/navigation';
  let selected = $state(null);

  async function openPhoto(id) {
    // ❌ OLD: A real navigation. This runs the target route's load
    // functions, fetches data, and swaps the whole page component —
    // heavyweight for something that should be an overlay on top of
    // the current list.
    await goto(`/photos/${id}`); // ❌ OLD: full route change
  }
</script>

<!-- The list page unmounts, the photo route mounts; back navigation
     re-runs the list load and loses scroll position. -->

<script>
  import { pushState } from '$app/navigation';
  import { page } from '$app/state';

  let selected = $state(null);

  function openPhoto(id) {
    // ✅ NEW: update the URL + history WITHOUT loading anything.
    // The list stays mounted; the modal opens on top.
    selected = id;
    pushState(new URL(`/photos/${id}`, location.href), { modal: id }); // ✅ NEW
  }

  function closePhoto() {
    selected = null;
    pushState(new URL('/photos', location.href)); // ✅ NEW: restore the URL
  }

  // $page.state.modal tells you which photo the URL says is open, and
  // the browser back button returns to the previous URL state.

interviewGotchas.question: What exactly does pushState NOT do that goto does, and why does that matter for modals?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This tests the navigation pipeline distinction — interviewers want you to enumerate what a full navigation triggers (load, component swap) and why shallow routing avoids each for ephemeral UI state.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: goto (full navigation) runs the navigation pipeline: it resolves the new route, calls its load functions (fetching data), potentially invokes guards, swaps the component tree, and updates the document. pushState bypasses all of that: it only calls history.pushState, updates the $page url/state, and leaves the current component and its data untouched. For a modal, that is exactly right — the overlay is UI state layered on the current page, not a new page. Full navigation would unmount the list, re-fetch data on return, and lose scroll position. Shallow routing also makes the modal's state part of the URL: refresh restores the URL (and you can re-open the modal from it), and the back button naturally closes it because the previous history entry is the closed state.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'pushState is just a faster goto'. It does not run load at all — that's a semantic difference, not a speed one. Another trap: expecting the new URL to reflect server state or trigger data updates — it won't, and code that relies on load running will silently keep stale data. Candidates who enumerate the skipped pipeline steps show real understanding.

interviewGotchas.question: How do you restore modal state on refresh with shallow routing, and what role does $page.state play?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This probes the state-recovery pattern — interviewers want to know how the URL becomes the source of truth for ephemeral UI after a page reload, which is the point of URL-syncing modals.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: On refresh, the URL is the only thing that survives — the in-memory modal state is gone. To restore, your page reads $page.url (and $page.state) during initialization: if the URL path/query indicates a modal (e.g. /photos/1), re-open the modal and load its content. The state argument passed to pushState is stored on the history entry and available via $page.state after back/forward navigation, but on a hard refresh the state object is NOT restored (only the URL is) — so recovery must be driven primarily from the URL, with $page.state as supplementary ephemeral data. The robust pattern: derive modal-openness from the URL, not from component state alone, so refresh, share, and back-button all behave consistently.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is '$page.state survives a refresh'. History state does not survive a full page reload — only the URL does. Another trap: storing non-serializable data in the state argument — the History API requires structured-cloneable values. Candidates who center recovery on the URL and treat state as ephemeral show real production experience.
